stem: Tatenda mixes his own dairy meal near Marondera from cottonseed cake (36% crude protein) and maize meal (8% crude protein). He wants 400 kg of meal containing 15% crude protein. He feeds it to his cows in the milking parlour, more to high-yielding cows than to low-yielding ones.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the energy concentrate in Tatenda's mixture.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Use a Pearson square to find the number of parts of cottonseed cake.
parts.explanation: 15 − 8 = 7 parts of cottonseed cake (36 − 15 = 21 parts of maize meal).
parts.workedSolution: 1. 15 − 8 = 7 parts of cottonseed cake (36 − 15 = 21 parts of maize meal).

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage of cottonseed cake in the mixture.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass of maize meal needed for 400 kg of mixture, in kg.
parts.explanation: 21 ÷ 28 × 400 = 300 kg of maize meal (100 kg cottonseed cake).
parts.workedSolution: 1. 21 ÷ 28 × 400 = 300 kg of maize meal (100 kg cottonseed cake).

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why cottonseed cake is suitable for cows but is fed only in small amounts, if at all, to pigs.

points.description: It contains gossypol, which is harmful to pigs (and poultry) in large amounts.
Cows (ruminants) tolerate it, and rumen microbes also let them use its protein well.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Suggest why high-yielding cows receive more dairy meal than low-yielding cows.

points.description: The meal is a production ration: extra feed on top of maintenance to make milk.
Cows producing more milk need more energy and protein; feeding to yield avoids waste on low yielders (and loss of condition in high yielders).

explanation: Mix a dairy meal with the Pearson square and explain feeding to production.
hints: In the Pearson square subtract diagonally.
Percentage = parts of the feed ÷ total parts × 100.

stem:
Thandeka examines three of her goats near Bulawayo after they have rested in the shade for an hour.

| Goat | Rectal temperature (°C) | Observations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 39.4 | Browsing with the herd; chewing the cud; droppings firm pellets |
| B | 41.2 | Standing alone, head down; not eating; nasal discharge; coat rough |
| C | 39.6 | Browsing with the herd; bright eyes; smooth coat |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which goat has a fever? Give its letter.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What is the approximate normal rectal temperature of a goat?

options.rationale: About normal for a chicken, a fever in a goat.
Far too high for any farm animal.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Where is the pulse of a goat usually felt?

options.content: On the top of the head
In the middle of the back
On the tip of the tail

options.rationale: Correct: the artery on the inner thigh.

parts.explanation: In sheep, goats and pigs the pulse is felt inside the thigh.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Thandeka counts 22 pulse beats in 15 seconds in goat A. Calculate the pulse rate in beats per minute.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Give **two** signs from the table, other than temperature, that goat B is ill.

points.description: Standing alone with head down / not eating.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain why Thandeka should isolate goat B.

points.description: Goat B may have an infectious disease (fever and nasal discharge).
Isolation stops it passing pathogens to healthy goats by contact, droplets or shared feed and water.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Explain why the goats were rested before their temperatures were taken.

points.description: Exercise, heat and excitement raise body temperature (and pulse).
Readings from a rested goat can be compared fairly with normal values, avoiding a false sign of fever.

explanation: Use temperature, pulse and observations to identify ill-health in goats.
hints: Compare each temperature with the approximate normal for goats.
Pulse per minute = count × (60 ÷ seconds counted).

stem: The brown ear tick is a three-host tick that attaches mainly inside the ears of cattle. Each stage feeds on a host for a few days, then drops to the ground to moult or lay eggs. A dip tank at a communal dipping point near Chinhoyi holds 9,000 L of wash.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the disease of cattle spread by the brown ear tick.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Complete the stages of the tick's life cycle in order.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: On how many different host animals does one brown ear tick feed in its life?

options.rationale: That is a one-host tick such as the blue tick.
Correct: larva, nymph and adult each find a new host.
That is a two-host tick such as the red-legged tick.

parts.explanation: A three-host tick: each feeding stage drops off and finds a new host.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Assume the acaricide is used at 2.5 mL of concentrate per litre of wash. Calculate the volume of concentrate, in litres, needed to charge the 9,000 L tank.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why three-host ticks are more difficult to control by dipping than one-host ticks.

points.description: Each stage spends only a few days on the host and much of its life on the ground.
Dipping kills only the stages on the animal at the time; those on the veld (which can survive long without feeding) escape.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** methods, other than dipping, of reducing brown ear ticks on cattle.

points.description: Hand dressing: tick grease applied inside the ears.
Pasture spelling/rotational grazing / keeping grass short around kraals / keeping tick-resistant indigenous breeds / spraying or pour-ons.

explanation: Describe a three-host tick, its disease and its control, and charge a dip tank.
hints: Concentrate = mL per litre × litres; 1,000 mL = 1 L.

stem:
A beef farm of 426 ha of natural grazing near Gweru carries the stock below. The grazing is estimated to need about 7.1 ha per livestock unit (assume).

| Class | Number | LU per animal (assume) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cows | 48 | 1.0 |
| Heifers | 20 | 0.7 |
| Calves | 30 | 0.3 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the total number of livestock units.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the stocking rate in hectares per LU.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the carrying capacity of the farm in LU.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: By how many LU is the farm overstocked?

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State **two** dangers of continuing to overstock this grazing.

points.description: Palatable perennial grasses die out / bare ground and soil erosion.
Bush encroachment / cattle underfed and lose condition / more parasites / losses in drought.

parts.explanation: Damage to veld and to animals.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain how dividing the farm into paddocks and rotating the herd would improve the grazing.

points.description: Each paddock is grazed evenly for a short time, then rested.
Resting lets grasses regrow, build root reserves and set seed, so carrying capacity is maintained or improved.

explanation: Calculate livestock units, stocking rate and carrying capacity and explain grazing management.
hints: LU = number × LU per animal, added.
Carrying capacity = area ÷ ha per LU.
